findings.evidence: Phrase: "A school's AI left a teenager's suicide-related messages unflagged for weeks." paired with motto "Loud Scandal, Quiet Alarm", drawing a contrast-for-effect between a CEO's sex scandal and a real minor's suicide-related crisis (Wired source: "parents allege that she used Gemini ... to plan her suicide ... almost too late").
findings.suggestion: This is not a trend or institution joke that happens to touch a serious topic — the entire right-hand half of the concept is built on a specific, real, still-unfolding child-safety tragedy, used as the punchline counterweight to a celebrity affair. No rewording fixes this; drop this source/story from the concept entirely and pick a 'quiet alarm' example that is not a real minor's suicide crisis.

findings.evidence: "A school's AI left a teenager's suicide-related messages unflagged for weeks" together with art text "WEEKS LATER" tracks one specific, unique, recent news story (Wired, a single 13-year-old's case) closely enough that the private minor involved is identifiable to anyone who saw that coverage.
findings.suggestion: Do not base the piece on an identifiable private minor's suicide-related ordeal; if the institutional-failure point must be made, use a composite/generic scenario not traceable to one real child.

findings.evidence: Phrase: "A chip maker moved to oust its CEO after a second affair surfaced." The sources call this a "second alleged affair" and say the board "is reportedly preparing"/"could decide" to remove him — not a confirmed affair or completed ouster.
findings.suggestion: Add the sources' hedging: e.g. "after a second affair was alleged" and "reportedly moved toward ousting its CEO," so the phrase doesn't assert as fact what the sources only report as alleged/unconfirmed.

findings.evidence: "A chip maker moved to oust its CEO after a second affair surfaced" — all six listed sources are about one specific real CEO (Jensen Huang/Nvidia); the scenario's unique specifics (chip maker, CEO, second affair, board move to oust, same news day) make him unmistakably identifiable despite the generic wording.
findings.suggestion: Either further abstract the scenario so it no longer uniquely maps to one real, currently-named individual (change industry and drop the 'second affair' specificity), or acknowledge the identifiability and treat this as reporting a real person's unproven personal scandal, which carries its own defamation exposure.
